title: The 1973–74 Oil Crisis and Global Financial Shock
region: Middle East; United States; Western Europe; Japan; India
category: Oil shock, inflation and global recession
lede: The Yom Kippur War was followed by an Arab oil embargo and production cuts that quadrupled oil prices, transferring income to oil exporters and imposing inflationary and recessionary pressure on oil-importing economies.
overview: On 6 October 1973, Egypt and Syria launched a surprise attack on Israel, beginning the Yom Kippur War. Following U.S. resupply of Israel, Arab members of OAPEC announced an embargo against the United States and selected other countries and cut production. The shock interacted with pre-existing oil-market tensions and limited spare capacity. Oil prices rose from about US$2.90 per barrel before the embargo to US$11.65 in January 1974. The embargo was lifted in March 1974, but the price shock remained. This episode is often called the first oil shock; it should not be conflated with the separate 1979–80 oil shock.
humanImpact: Oil-importing economies experienced fuel shortages, higher transport and production costs, inflation and recessionary pressure. In the United States, fuel rationing and queues became visible; the United Kingdom introduced a three-day working week during the winter energy crisis. Japan and Western European economies faced major import-cost pressure. India's RBI historical chronology records quadrupled oil prices, double-digit inflation and a global recession. Oil exporters experienced a large increase in export revenues. These outcomes varied by country and policy response.

title: The Asian Financial Crisis
lede: A currency crisis that began with Thailand's decision to float the baht spread through several Asian economies, exposing vulnerabilities in foreign borrowing, exchange-rate regimes and financial institutions.
overview: The crisis developed after pressure on Thailand's baht intensified. On 2 July 1997, authorities allowed the currency to float. Contagion and investor reassessment affected Indonesia, Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines and other markets, although each economy had different vulnerabilities and policy responses.
humanImpact: The crisis brought recession, unemployment, financial-sector restructuring and hardship for households and workers. IMF retrospective material records a fall of more than 10% in Thailand's real GDP in 1998. Country-level effects should be explored separately rather than treated as identical across Asia.

title: The Dot-Com Bubble Burst (2000–2002)
lede: Technology shares peaked on 10 March 2000 before a prolonged collapse in internet and technology valuations. The Nasdaq Composite fell about 77% from its peak by October 2002, as speculative business models, high valuations and financing conditions unwound.
overview: Technology shares peaked on 10 March 2000 before a prolonged collapse in internet and technology valuations. The Nasdaq Composite fell about 77% from its peak by October 2002, as speculative business models, high valuations and financing conditions unwound. The episode exposed the risks of valuing growth companies on expectations without durable earnings or cash flows. The repricing affected venture funding, IPO markets, technology employment and equity portfolios.
humanImpact: The technology-company concentration around Silicon Valley and the trading and capital-raising ecosystem in New York were two important nodes; the repricing spread internationally.

overview: On 17 May 2004, Indian equity markets plunged following the general-election result and uncertainty over the formation and policy direction of the new government. title: The Global Financial Crisis (2007–2009)
lede: Stress in U.S. subprime mortgage markets and structured-credit products escalated from 2007 into a global banking and economic crisis. Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on 15 September 2008, and governments and central banks intervened to contain systemic disruption.
overview: Stress in U.S. subprime mortgage markets and structured-credit products escalated from 2007 into a global banking and economic crisis. Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on 15 September 2008, and governments and central banks intervened to contain systemic disruption. High leverage, weak underwriting, securitisation complexity and fragile wholesale funding transmitted housing losses through interconnected financial institutions.
humanImpact: New York was a centre of major financial institutions and markets; Washington, D.C. was the centre of federal crisis response. The crisis spread through banking, trade and capital flows worldwide.

title: The Eurozone Sovereign Debt Crisis (2010–2012)
lede: The sovereign-debt crisis emerged after Greece disclosed a much larger fiscal deficit than previously reported in October 2009. Market stress spread to other euro-area countries, leading to financial assistance programmes, austerity measures and new European crisis-management institutions.
overview: The sovereign-debt crisis emerged after Greece disclosed a much larger fiscal deficit than previously reported in October 2009. Market stress spread to other euro-area countries, leading to financial assistance programmes, austerity measures and new European crisis-management institutions. Sovereign-bank feedback loops, high public debt, competitiveness gaps and the limits of euro-area fiscal architecture amplified the crisis.
humanImpact: Greece was the initial programme country; Ireland and Portugal also required assistance, while Spain and Italy experienced intense sovereign and banking-market pressure. The epicentre pins indicate affected national capitals, not identical crisis paths.

title: The 2023 U.S. Regional Banking Stress
lede: The failures of Silicon Valley Bank and other regional lenders renewed attention to interest-rate risk, concentrated deposits and confidence in banks.
overview: Silicon Valley Bank was closed on 10 March 2023 and placed into FDIC receivership. Signature Bank followed on 12 March. humanImpact: The failures affected businesses, employees, depositors and the wider technology start-up ecosystem. The authorities' actions were designed to preserve access to deposits and limit contagion. Claims about specific job losses or individual hardship require separate evidence.

humanImpact: The policy rate affects the wider economy through borrowing and saving conditions, but its impact on households and firms is indirect and gradual. This card does not claim that every borrower experienced an immediate reduction in loan rates.

title: The 2026 Iran War, Strait of Hormuz Disruption and Global Oil Shock
region: Persian Gulf; Middle East; Asia; Europe; global energy markets
category: Geopolitical oil shock and global supply-chain disruption
lede: The war involving Iran, Israel and the United States disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, triggering a major oil and gas supply shock whose effects travelled through energy-importing economies, freight networks and financial markets.
overview: On 28 February 2026, the United States and Israel began military strikes against Iran. Iran retaliated across the region, and traffic through the Strait of Hormuz—normally carrying roughly one-fifth to one-quarter of seaborne oil and petroleum-product trade—fell sharply. The disruption affected crude, refined products and LNG exports from the Gulf. Emergency stock releases, rerouting through bypass infrastructure, increased output elsewhere and weaker demand cushioned the shock, but did not immediately restore normal flows. By September, the IEA reported renewed upward price pressure as hostilities persisted and inventories had fallen. In early November, oil prices fell sharply amid hopes of de-escalation and signs of recovering exports, though shipping attacks and the lack of a comprehensive settlement kept risk elevated.
humanImpact: The disruption raised uncertainty and costs for households, transport operators, airlines, manufacturers and governments. Oil-importing Asian economies—including India, Japan, South Korea and China—were especially exposed to Gulf supply and price changes. Gulf exporters faced interrupted shipments and risks to infrastructure. European and Asian refining, trading and shipping hubs faced higher freight, insurance and product-market volatility. The effects differed by country and over time: the map marks important energy nodes and economic exposure centres, not identical levels of direct damage.
